rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Samarrāʾ distinguishes fronting a word before its own governor from reordering words relative to each other.
rows.anchor: تقديم اللفظ على عامله نحو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting before a word's governor usually marks exclusivity: ‘I helped Khālid’ does not, while ‘Khālid I helped’ singles him out.
rows.anchor: وهذا التقديم في الغالب يفيد الاختصاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object ‘You’ is fronted with worship and seeking help because these belong exclusively to God; worship is similarly exclusive in 39:66 and 2:172.
rows.anchor: على فعل العبادة وعلى فعل الاستعانة دون فعل الهداية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting the prepositional phrase with trust and turning to God signals exclusivity: reliance is on Him alone, and turning back is only to Him.
rows.anchor: فقدم الجار والمجرور للدلالة على الاختصاص وذلك لأن التوكل لا يكون إلا على الله وحده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request for guidance is not exclusive: one cannot ask God to guide only oneself and leave everyone else unguided, as with requests for provision, healing, and well-being.
rows.anchor: ولم يقدم مفعول الهداية على فعله فلم يقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ‘we believe in Him and trust in Him,’ belief is not restricted to God because it includes other required articles, while trust is exclusively in God and is therefore fronted.
rows.anchor: قدم الجار والمجرور فيه ليؤذن باختصاص التوكل من العبد على الله دون غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second kind rearranges words that are not moved before their own governor; the placement of ‘what is offered to other than God’ varies with context.
rows.anchor: الثاني: تقديم الألفاظ بعضها على بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronted destinations in these return passages express that return and final gathering are to God alone, with no other destination.
rows.anchor: فالمساق إلى الله وحده لا إلى ذات أخرى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some explain the fronting as matching the verse endings; Samarrāʾ rejects this and says it marks exclusivity.
rows.anchor: وهذا ليس من التقديم من أجل مراعاة المشاكلة لرؤوس الآي كما ذهب بعضهم بل هو لقصد الاختصاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Preposing the locative with knowledge of the Hour marks that this knowledge belongs exclusively to God.
rows.anchor: فعلم الساعة مختص بالله وحده لا يعلمه أحد غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ‘with Him are the keys of the unseen,’ fronting the predicate signals God's exclusive knowledge, reinforced by the explicit restriction ‘none knows them but He.’
rows.anchor: فقدم الظرف الذي هو الخبر على المبتدأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting may also serve praise, glorification, magnification, or disparagement, although exclusivity is its most common effect.
rows.anchor: وقد يكون التقديم من هذا النوع لغرض آخر كالمدح والثناء والتعظيم والتحقير وغير ذلك من الأغراض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting Noah in ‘and Noah We guided before’ praises him; it does not mean God guided no one else.
rows.anchor: فهذا ليس من باب التخصيص إذ ليس معناه أننا ما هدينا إلا نوحا وإنما هو من باب المدح والثناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orphan and petitioner are foregrounded for attention and guidance because they are vulnerable and liable to be oppressed, not to license mistreatment of others.
rows.anchor: فإن اليتيم ضعيف وكذلك السائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Word order follows the occasion and context; saying only that a word receives attention is too vague unless one explains why this context favors it over alternatives.
rows.anchor: فإذا أردت أن تبين أسباب هذا التقديم أو ذاك فإنه لا يصح الاكتفاء بالقول إنه قدم هذه الكلمة هنا للعناية بها والاهتمام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an considers each word across all its occurrences, producing a coherent whole and placing each expression where the context and overall pattern suit it.
rows.anchor: بل راعى جميع المواضع التي وردت فيها اللفظة ونظر إليها نظرة واحدة شاملة في القرآن الكريم كله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an varies whether sky or earth, people or jinn, harm or benefit comes first according to what each passage calls for.
rows.anchor: فنراه مثلاً يقدم السماء على الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some ordering follows temporal priority: jinn before humans, drowsiness before sleep, ʿĀd before Thamūd, night before day, and darkness before light; jinn's earlier creation is stated in 15:27.
rows.anchor: حسب القدم والأولية في الوجود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parallel Moses passages differ because al-Baqara recounts blessings to Israel, while al-Aʿrāf reproaches a people who repeatedly disobeyed after rescue, demanded idols, worshipped the calf, and violated the Sabbath.
rows.anchor: فسياق هذه الآيات في سورة البقرة هو تعداد النعم التي أنعمها الله على بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passages vary in active versus passive speech, ‘enter’ versus ‘settle,’ the food command, ‘freely,’ the order of entry and prostration, the spelling of ‘sins,’ the punishment verbs and cause, and ‘gushed’ versus ‘welled.’
rows.anchor: وإذا استسقى موسى لقومه إذ استسقاه قومه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Baqara says ‘when We said,’ attributing the command to God in its blessing context; al-Aʿrāf uses the passive ‘when it was said to them’ in its reproach context.
rows.anchor: فأسند الرب القول إلى نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an attributes blessing and good to God as honor and grace, while avoiding direct attribution of evil to Him, often using a passive form.
rows.anchor: والقرآن الكريم يسند الفعل إلى الله سبحانه في مقام التشريف والتكريم ومقام الخير العام والتفضل بخلاف الشر والسوء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Fātiḥa explicitly attributes favor to God (‘You bestowed favor’) while describing the blameworthy as those under anger and those astray.
rows.anchor: صِرَاطَ الذين أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ غَيْرِ المغضوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham attributes creation, guidance, food, drink, and healing to God, but says ‘when I am ill’ rather than ascribing illness to God.
rows.anchor: فأنت ترى أنه نسب الخير إلى ربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn statement leaves the intended harm passive but directly says their Lord intends right guidance, distinguishing evil from good attribution.
rows.anchor: فبنى إرادة الشر للمجهول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the boat episode, the speaker says ‘I wanted to damage it,’ taking responsibility for the apparent harm rather than attributing it to God.
rows.anchor: فقال في خرق السفينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boy's killing and replacement combine apparent evil with good, so the speaker says ‘we wanted’; the good replacement is then attributed to the boy's Lord alone.
rows.anchor: أما في قتل الغلام فجاء بالضمير مشتركاً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because raising the wall is wholly good, the speaker attributes it to God alone: ‘your Lord wanted.’
rows.anchor: فأسنده إلى الله سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God explicitly ascribes beautifying faith and the adorned heavens to Himself; beautification of worldly desires and sinful deeds is generally passive, and the text does not say ‘We beautified their evil deeds.’
rows.anchor: فأنت ترى أنه ينسب تزيين الخير إلى نفسه بخلاف تزيين السوء
